        Pursuant to Rules 206(f) and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 the Midcontinent Independent

System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) submits this Answer to the June 22, 2026 complaint filed in the

above-captioned docket by American Transmission Company LLC (“ATC”).2 The Complaint

 alleges that MISO misapplied its Tariff3 in administering the Competitive Developer Selection

Process4 for the Wisconsin Southeast Competitive Transmission Project (“WISE” or “Project

WISE”), a Multi-Value Project (“MVP”) that was included in MISO’s Long Range Transmission

Planning (“LRTP”) Tranche 2.1 and MISO Transmission Expansion Plan 2024 (“MTEP24”).5 As

a remedy for MISO’s alleged missteps, the Complaint requests that the Commission direct MISO

to “re-administer” the competitive bid process for the portion of Project WISE that was assigned

to Viridon Midcontinent, LLC (“Viridon”), the winning Project WISE bidder.6 Because ATC has

failed to demonstrate any Tariff violation by MISO, the Commission should deny the relief sought

in the Complaint.7

I.        EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

          The Complaint rests on incorrect assumptions about the timing, documentation, and

relevance of proposed in-service dates (“ISDs”) for the three WISE substations included in ATC’s

Ozaukee County Transmission Project,8 as well as erroneous understandings surrounding MISO’s

Tariff prescribed processes, the Competitive Transmission Project Proposal evaluation criteria,

and the awarded Selected Proposal. While MISO appreciates ATC’s frustration that the Tariff did

not allow MISO to effectuate ATC’s preferred resolution, MISO worked collaboratively with ATC

         MISO acknowledges ATC’s load-serving obligations, including with respect to the

proposed Ozaukee County Data Center and the need for ATC to construct the Ozaukee Country

Transmission Project to facilitate that interconnection.10 The implications of the rapid growth of

large loads have been a significant industry challenge and put renewed pressure on existing

practices and processes in MISO and other transmission provider regions. These challenges,

however, do not give MISO license to operate outside of the Tariff. There is an ongoing

stakeholder and FERC process to address various aspects of large load interconnections, but MISO

cannot simply override the existing Tariff requirements governing the Competitive Developer

Selection Process to instantaneously prioritize ATC’s Ozaukee Country Transmission Project with

no regard to its obligations as the administrator of the Competitive Developer Selection Process.

 As a public utility, MISO is required to follow its Tariff and, where necessary, exercise discretion

in a non-discriminatory fashion. This has been done in the Project WISE case.

         It should be noted that the Tariff includes certain tools to address unique challenges that

may arise in the Competitive Transmission Process. One such tool is the Variance Analysis

process, which allows MISO to promptly address contingencies such as schedule delays, inability

to construct, and regulatory and permitting challenges.11 Facing a post-award change in Project

WISE’s scope, MISO followed the Variance Analysis process using all available information as

appropriate. Consistent with the Tariff, that process addressed the issue raised by ATC by

reassigning the three Substations needed for the Ozaukee Country Transmission Project to ATC,

thereby accommodating its desired in-service dates for these facilities. The process worked and

MISO was clear in its conversations with ATC with respect to all applicable Tariff requirements,

consistent with its role as the neutral administrator of the Competitive Developer Selection

Process.

         In the Answer below, MISO demonstrates that it punctually adhered to all Tariff-prescribed

requirements applicable to the issuance of the Request for Proposals (“RFP”) for Project WISE.

The Answer also explains that MISO’s thorough and robust evaluation of the submitted WISE

proposals and ultimate determination of the WISE Selected Developer was appropriate and

conforming to the Tariff. Overall, MISO conducted its Competitive Developer Selection Process

in accordance with the Tariff, the MISO Transmission Owners Agreement (“TOA”),12 and the

requirements set forth in Orders Nos. 890 and 1000 and as openly and transparently based on the

          The Commission should deny the Complaint. ATC’s requested relief—rerunning the

competitive process for the WISE project or revising evaluation standards—would conflict with

the Tariff, disrupt timely transmission development, and undermine the transparency and integrity

of the competitive framework. MISO recognizes that the industry evolves and new challenges

need to be met. The MISO stakeholder process is designed to allow stakeholders to identify and

bring new solutions to address such challenges.

          Additionally, MISO has consistently looked to enhance the competitive solicitation process

and is also looking at broader enhancements to support large load integration in a reliable, cost

effective and efficient manner. To that end, MISO will commit to a review with stakeholders,

opportunities to enhance its competitive solicitation processes to most effectively manage the

uncertainty and speed to power with the rapid growth in large loads in light of the Commission’s

existing Order No. 1000 requirements.

II.       RELEVANT BACKGROUND

          A.      MISO’s Competitive Transmission Process

                  1. Overall Structure and Design

          In Order No. 1000, the Commission required transmission providers to conduct

competitive solicitations for regional transmission projects. The Commission agreed with the

economic principle that “competition will normally lead to lower prices,”13 as well as “improved

these requirements in its Order No. 1000 compliance proceedings15 by including the Competitive

Developer Selection Process and the Variance Analysis process in the MISO Transmission

Expansion Planning Protocol set forth in Attachment FF of the Tariff. By following the procedures

established in Attachment FF of the Tariff and the TOA Planning Framework,16 MISO provides

an open and transparent regional planning process, which results in recommendations for

expansion that are reported in the MTEP and ensures that all participants in this process are treated

fairly and without undue discrimination or unlawful preference.

         As detailed in Attachment FF and MISO’s Business Practices Manuals (“BPM”),17 MISO

develops the MTEP, its annual regional expansion plan, based on expected use patterns and

analysis of the performance of the Transmission System in meeting both reliability needs and the

needs of the competitive bulk power market, under a wide variety of contingency conditions.18 All

individual projects proposed to be included in the MTEP are thoroughly reviewed by MISO’s

stakeholders and planning staff and, based on that review, may be recommended to the MISO

Board of Directors (“MISO Board”) for approval on a biennial basis, or more frequently if needed.

         After the MISO Board approves an MTEP, the Competitive Developer Selection Process

begins. The first step in that process is the review and apply the applicable exceptions of the

Competitive Developer Selection Process, and then publicly identify the Competitive

the MTEP approval21 from Qualified Transmission Developers to construct, implement, own,

operate, maintain, repair, and restore the Competitive Transmission Facilities; (2) the submission

evaluation of submitted Proposals within the Tariff-provided timeframe of 165 Calendar Days;23

and (4) designation of a Selected Proposal and Selected Developer(s).24

          MISO evaluates each Proposal utilizing the Evaluation Principles and the evaluation

criteria as set forth in the Tariff, along with the application of reasonable judgment and opinion,

within one hundred and sixty-five (165) Calendar Days from the respective Proposal Submission

Deadline.37 The Proposals are evaluated by MISO and/or its expert consultants overseen by the

MISO Competitive Transmission Executive Committee (“CTEC”), which has the exclusive and

final authority to determine the Selected Proposal.38 The evaluation of Proposals is guided and

influenced by the collective application of the MISO Evaluation Principles set forth in BPM-027,

which are intended to provide a framework for applying the evaluation criteria specified by the

MISO Tariff to score each Proposal being evaluated. The MISO Evaluation Principles include:

(1) certainty: providing a high degree of certainty and predictability; (2) risk mitigation: reflecting

the lowest risk to the success of the project; (3) cost: meeting all requirements at the lowest overall

cost; and (4) specificity: providing a high degree of specificity and detail.39 RFP Respondents that

clearly articulate how the various aspects of their Proposal provide certainty, specificity, reduces

and/or mitigates risk, and lowers cost will be advantaged.

Substation Facilities.40 The type of evaluation weighting will determine the maximum amount of

                   3.        Selection Report and Selected Developer Agreement

           MISO announces the Selected Developer(s) within 165 Calendar Days of the Proposal

           C.     Project WISE

MTEP24 included a portfolio of MVPs, which were selected and approved as a part of MISO’s

transmission system.
